conversation.content: Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll use a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to get a quick picture of your emotional well-being over the past seven days. It’s completely confidential, there are no right or wrong answers, and we can pause any time. It’s just ten questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally. When you’re ready, we’ll start.
Hi Sarah. I’ve heard of this from my midwife—happy to answer whatever you need. I’m ready when you are.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Most of the time I still laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before I had the baby, but yeah, I can still find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like when my sister comes over or when I get a quiet moment to drink a hot coffee—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. A lot of the time I’m too tired to really enjoy much.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Yeah… sometimes I catch myself thinking it’s my fault if she won’t settle or if I can’t get her to nap. I know logically it’s not really on me, but in the moment I do wonder what I’m doing wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

It happens—like I’ll suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay in the bassinet or if I’m producing enough milk even when everything looks fine. I can usually shake it off, but it pops up a few times a week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky, but there’ve been a couple of moments—usually at night—where my chest gets tight and I feel this rush of “something bad is going to happen,” even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me
Some days, yeah. When she’s cluster-feeding and the house is a mess and I haven’t showered, it feels like I’m barely treading water. I manage, but I end those days pretty wiped out and teary.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy, but I do have trouble sleeping a few nights a week—mostly because my mind keeps running through baby stuff or I’m listening for every little sound she makes. Once I do drift off I’m usually OK, but dropping off is hard.
I have felt sad or miserable
I get spells of that—especially in the evenings when I’m really tired—but it’s not all day, every day. It comes and goes, maybe every other day or so.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve only cried once this week—one night when she wouldn’t latch and I was exhausted. It wasn’t an all-day thing, just a short meltdown after which I felt a bit better.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I might feel overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that, while you can still laugh and find moments to enjoy, the sparkle isn't quite the same since your baby arrived. Evenings feel heavy: you're tired, teary, and sometimes overwhelmed by everyday tasks, and worries about your baby's safety or your milk supply pop up several nights a week. You're managing, but it's clear that some days feel like you're "barely treading water," and brief, unsettling surges of panic have caught you off-guard. At the same time, you remain firmly connected to your support network and have never considered self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and excitement compared to before, matching 'Definitely less than I used to'.</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "sometimes" when baby won't settle, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring, unfounded worries several times per week, consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes episodic, unexpected anxiety episodes that meet "scared/panicky without cause," matching "Yes, sometimes" in frequency and intensity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed on some days, struggling to cope, matching "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, recurring spells of sadness every other day, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 15 falls within the "probable depression" range (≥14) and meets provisional screening criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: core mood symptoms (<sym>low mood</sym> most evenings), <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>not the same excitement</quote>), guilt/self-blame, anxiety, and associated sleep disturbance. Frequency and functional impact (fatigue, household tasks "getting on top") support clinical concern despite retained partial enjoyment. No self-harm ideation lowers acute safety risk but does not negate need for evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for full diagnostic assessment
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment options (therapy, consider medication if moderate-severe)
3. Share results with maternity care team for coordinated support and follow-up
4. Plan daily rest windows and accept practical help to reduce fatigue
5. Use brief grounding techniques when <sym>chest tightness or dread</sym> appears
6. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks or sooner if mood worsens, hopelessness emerges, or any self-harm thoughts develop
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum parent (infant ≤12 mo)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia (reduced enjoyment)  
- Episodic low mood, tearfulness, “spells” of sadness, worst in evenings  
- Self-blame when infant fussy/not sleeping  
- Nocturnal anxiety (breathing, milk supply) 3–4×/week  
- Two brief nocturnal panic-like episodes (chest tightness, dread)  
- Sleep-onset insomnia ruminating about infant care  
- Feeling “overwhelmed,” “barely treading water,” end-of-day tearfulness  

Functional impact  
- Fatigue, interrupted sleep, decreased self-care, household tasks “getting on top” of her  
- No self-harm ideation; no suicidal thoughts reported

Pattern  
Symptoms fluctuate, not pervasive; worst when fatigued or cluster-feeding. No prior psychiatric history reported in this screen.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for Perinatal Depression and Anxiety: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety, sleep disturbance. Does not meet threshold for severe major depression (no anhedonia “all day,” no daily crying, no suicidal ideation).  
Risk factors: fatigue, infant care stress, sleep deprivation.  
Protective factors: retains some enjoyment, social support (sister), denies self-harm.

Recommendation  
Continue monitoring with EPDS at next visit; consider brief counseling, psycho-education, sleep-hygiene, and maternal respite supports. Re-screen sooner if symptoms worsen, daily crying, hopelessness, or any self-harm ideation develop.
